item.title: An Ancient Wall Sheds Light On an Old Question: Where Did Paris Begin?
item.description:
An ancient wall, discovered recently during excavations to shore up a hospital in Paris, could help clarify the location of the city’s original settlements around the time that Julius Caesar chronicled the Roman conquest of Gaul, according to experts.

The stone and wood wall, which measures 72 feet, is characteristic of Gallic fortifications dating from the late Iron Age, which ended around the first century B.C. The structure was found this summer, along with a Gallic spearhead, at a construction site inside the hospital Hôtel Dieu, on the Île de la Cité, an island on the Seine River in the heart of Paris.

The French culture minister, Catherine Pégard, described it in a statement on Wednesday as “one of the most important archaeological remains ever discovered for understanding Gallic Lutetia.”

Lutetia, the Latin name for the city that would eventually become Paris, was built by a Gallic tribe that lived along the Seine River probably as early as the fourth century B.C. Julius Caesar, in his chronicle of the Gallic Wars — the Roman campaigns fought between 58 and 50 B.C. against tribes in Gaul — described Lutetia as a fortification built on an island in the Seine. Rome conquered the city in 52 B.C.

In his account, Caesar describes Roman legions moving “for Lutetia, a town of the Parisii, situated on an island in the river Seine.” He adds that Gallic tribes, learning of the Roman advance, had “ordered Lutetia to be set on fire and the bridges belonging to the town to be cut down.”

Until now, Caesar’s vague description and the lack of archaeological evidence made the location of a Gallic city on the Seine a source of debate among French scholars. Many questioned whether Lutetia was located in the heart of Paris or somewhere else. Some argued that the settlement was actually in Nanterre, a suburb west of Paris, citing archaeological discoveries there in the 1990s.

“I was among the colleagues who wrote that Lutetia was probably not located on the Île de la Cité, since at the time — in the 1990s — the evidence was really very, very scant,” said Matthieu Poux, an archaeology professor at the University of Lyon II.

But the finding of the wall had changed his mind, Mr. Poux said, adding that he now had no doubt that the location of the ancient city was on the Île de la Cité.

While Ms. Pégard, the culture minister, said further scientific research was needed to verify the wall’s “function and its chronology,” initial carbon dating of wood fragments indicates that the wall dates back to between 200 B.C. and 10 B.C., which matches the period chronicled by Julius Caesar.

Moreover, the wall bears traces of a fire, potentially in keeping with Caesar’s account. “Charred seeds and the remains of a burned wooden building were also unearthed,” the culture ministry said, which may correspond to Caesar’s account that the Gauls set fire to their settlement before fleeing the advancing Romans.

Archaeological finds have shed significant light on the development of Roman-era Lutetia. Roman artifacts have been found under what is today the Latin Quarter, and a Roman residential area was uncovered under the Luxembourg Gardens, roughly a mile south of the Île de la Cité.

Much less was known about Gallic Lutetia. But, as Mr. Poux said, this discovery under the hospital “increases the amount of data available on this topic tenfold in a single excavation campaign.”

The finding, he said, could be a “starting point” for other archaeological discoveries on the Île de la Cité, though he noted that digs are limited to ongoing refurbishment of buildings, slowing the progress.

The culture ministry said further excavations would take place in the vicinity of the site, and that the entire wall would ultimately be moved to be studied and displayed. Emmanuel Grégoire, the mayor of Paris, said the city would “share this heritage with the people of Paris and all of those who cherish the city.”

item.title: Canada’s Capital Bids Good Riddance to Trump Avenue as Tensions With U.S. Rise
item.description:
Call it the lake effect.

Take away a body of water steeped in Canadian pride, as President Trump attempted when he ordered the federal government last month to rename Lake Ontario as Lake America, and reprisals from the north seemed bound to follow. Even from reputedly mild-mannered Canadians.

A backlash on a smaller scale came on Wednesday when the City Council in Ottawa, Canada’s capital, voted unanimously to remove Trump Avenue as the name of a residential street, the latest in a cross-border geographic spat that is making mapmakers’ heads spin.

The street is one of several in Ottawa’s Central Park neighborhood that were named for New York City institutions when it was developed in the late 1990s and early 2000s, long before Mr. Trump started a trade war with one of America’s closest allies.

And long before Mr. Trump audaciously suggested making Canada the “51st state” and imposed crippling tariffs on it.

“I don’t like the idea of anything that’s named for Donald Trump, who has demonstrated hostility towards Canada,” Mark Sutcliffe, Ottawa’s mayor and a council member, said at news conference after the vote.

The motion passed unanimously to change the name of the S-shaped street, which has about 65 homes on it and intersects with some other roads whose names might be familiar to New Yorkers, including Whitestone Drive and Bloomingdale Street.

John Germano, 65, a retiree who has lived on Trump Avenue since 2010, said in a phone interview on Wednesday that his address had become a dubious distinction, especially when ordering deliveries.

“It’s embarrassing, like they just chuckle and laugh,” Mr. Germano said.

He added, “It gets worse and worse every day.”

A working group of several Trump Avenue residents will help create a list of potential replacement names, said Riley Brockington, a City Council member who is spearheading the change.

Mr. Brockington said the erasure of Mr. Trump’s name from the street was not intended as retaliation for Mr. Trump’s bid to rename Lake Ontario but in response to what he described as the president’s attacks on Canadian sovereignty and the carnage caused by his economic policies.

“He does not deserve the honor of having his name on a city of Ottawa street,” Mr. Brockington said. “We’re the nation’s capital.”

The White House did not immediately respond to a request for comment on Wednesday.

Pete Hoekstra, the United States ambassador to Canada, who has been the subject of a petition effort seeking to expel him that has been signed by more than 200,000 Canadians, declined to comment on Wednesday.

Canada has at least eight other places with the name Trump in them, though those are not named after the president. Still, some have sought to change those names, too.

Two of them, East Trump Lake and West Trump Lake, can be found in Cochrane in eastern Ontario, according to the Canadian Geographical Names Database, which registered their origins in 1973.

Peter Politis, the mayor of Cochrane, said in an email on Wednesday that the lakes are in an unorganized township under provincial control. Not that renaming them hasn’t crossed his mind.

“That said, as mayor, I am sorely tempted to wave the mayoral pen and table a motion anyway, given how fitting it feels at the moment,” he wrote.

Mr. Politis mused that he might not stop there.

“On a tongue-in-cheek note, we’ve toyed with the idea of renaming our local landfill dump ‘Trump,’” he wrote.

Sudbury in Ontario is home to Trump Lake and Trump Creek, names that the Canadian Geographical Names Database recorded as originating in 1954.

Shortly after Mr. Trump’s executive action to rename Lake Ontario, Michel Lalonde, 36, a D.J. from the city of Sudbury, started a petition to rename Trump Lake. He said on Wednesday that he had never visited the lake, which is roughly six hours northwest of the city.

“The whole thing has become absurd and ridiculous,” he said.

Mr. Lalonde lamented the deterioration of U.S.-Canada relations.

“I just so wish we would go back to how things were 20 years ago,” he said. “It’s just an unfortunate stain on a relationship and an unfortunate stain on our history.”

In Ottawa, Mr. Brockington of the City Council said he had previously surveyed residents of Trump Avenue about changing the street’s name during the Covid-19 pandemic but they were divided. The opponents were concerned about the administrative hurdles associated with changing addresses, he said.

But after Mr. Trump returned to the White House and antagonized Canada, he said, momentum built for the change.

“This is not a tit for tat for Lake Ontario,” Mr. Brockington said. “At some point,” he added, “you have to take a stand.”

Mr. Germano said he was hoping to play a role in the selection of a new street name.

“We love New York,” he said. “We love Americans. It’s just that one person.”

He said he had kicked around some new names for Trump Avenue: Times Square, Strawberry Fields, Upper West Side.

“I’d go for Hell’s Kitchen,” he said.

item.title: Mark Carney’s Balancing Act
item.description:
Prime Minister Mark Carney of Canada said that he had prepared over the past year for the “extreme tail risk” that President Trump might order military action against Canada, but disclosed that the two men have spoken “frequently,” even since trade talks collapsed last month, describing a tense, evolving relationship.

In a wide-ranging interview with The New York Times at its headquarters in Midtown Manhattan on Wednesday, Mr. Carney described in meticulous detail how he was systematically reducing Canada’s reliance on the United States for key technology — from space satellites to fighter jets — in an effort to make his country far less vulnerable to American threats. He outlined a plan to diversify Canada’s relationships and suppliers, and said that even with a different future president “we will be a better partner for the U.S. because of what we are doing.”

He talked about reducing reliance on Starlink, Elon Musk’s satellite systems; considering alternatives to buying F-35 fighter jets; and a focus on deepening economic — though not defense — relationships with China. Mr. Trump’s exploitation of Canadian dependency on American products had taught the country a bitter lesson: “There’s certain things, once you’ve seen them, you can’t unsee them.”

When pressed on whether he took Mr. Trump’s threats to make Canada a 51st state seriously, Mr. Carney suggested that he had carefully examined the possibility of a U.S.-led military invasion, but declined to discuss in detail what that involved.

“I think you have a responsibility in these roles to look at extreme tail risk,” said Mr. Carney, a former central banker for Britain and Canada who approaches the world by meticulously assessing worst-case scenarios and drafting responses. He added: “That’s just risk management. That’s not a base case, but it would be irresponsible not to” prepare.

Mr. Carney spoke for an hour on a variety of challenges, including artificial intelligence, trade, and Canada’s role as a “middle power.”

Over the past year, he has emerged as the most prominent global leader to take on Mr. Trump. Along the way, he has also begun to define a path toward reducing dependence on a superpower neighbor that he has come to regard as predatory. Around the world, other leaders have looked to him as a model for dealing with an erratic, unreliable ally — one that remains, in Canada’s case, critical to national defense and economic survival.

But few of those leaders have articulated their interests as clearly as Mr. Carney, who used a speech at the World Economic Forum in Davos, Switzerland, earlier this year to describe a strategy for dealing with the rupture. “Either you retreat wholly into yourself or you diversify,” he said then, making the choice he faces stark.

Still, Mr. Carney said he speaks “frequently” to Mr. Trump and that they had spoken “a number of times” since trade talks broke down last month.

“From my perspective, we have a good relationship in the sense of we can pick up the phone and talk to each other about issues,” he said on Wednesday. “He’s direct. I’m direct in terms of where positions are. It’s much more efficient that way, and so you know that exists and that will continue to exist.”

The Canadian leader made the case, too, that in many ways, what’s good for Canada is also good for the United States because of their decades-long integration that has created stability and prosperity. Mr. Carney gave the example of the automobile industry, which is highly integrated across the U.S.-Canada border but has been at the center of the Trump administration’s tariff policy against Canada.

“My entire life, and I’m 61, we’ve had an integrated auto sector,” Mr. Carney said, adding that breaking that deep connection to repatriate all auto production to the United States is not good policy. “We think it doesn’t make sense,” he said.

Mr. Carney said that a path remains to resuming negotiations with the United States that would revive the trade agreement that fell apart in late August. Since then, the two countries have imposed rounds of tariffs on each other, and rhetoric has been menacing, particularly from Mr. Trump, who has repeatedly called Canada’s leadership “nasty.” But Mr. Carney brushed that off.

“Is there a mutually beneficial trade deal between Canada and the U.S.? Absolutely, absolutely there is one,” Mr. Carney said. He said that he was interested, for example, in adding potash to the talks. Canada provides almost 90 percent of all potash, the key ingredient for fertilizer, imported into the United States. Earlier this week, Mr. Trump said that he wanted to replace Canada’s supply with potash from Belarus — an authoritarian state aligned with Russia that is under U.S. sanctions for its role in the war in Ukraine.

Mr. Carney said that Canada, the United States and potentially also Mexico could become “fertilizer independent” by securing special access to Canada’s potash, the world’s largest reserve. He added that the Canadian option was clearly better than buying potash elsewhere that would then need to be transported through the Black Sea or the Strait of Hormuz.

“I think this is a doable component of the deal, and there are other examples that exist, and we’re ready to work toward,” he added.

At home, Mr. Carney has come under pressure to use Canada’s most sensitive and important export to the United States — energy — as leverage in the trade war. Some 60 percent of all oil imports into the United States come from Canada, while the country is also a major source of electricity for American households and industry.

Mr. Carney said he was very reluctant to limit, tariff or otherwise curb those exports to the United States.

“If you’re a reliable partner and you supply energy or food to somebody it keeps running, it’s a very, very, very high threshold to change that,” he said. “Never say never, but it starts from a position of, we need to be a reliable supplier in all cases.”

Although optimistic that efforts to strike a trade deal could be revived, Mr. Carney said he was cleareyed about areas where Canada needs to reduce its dependence on the United States.

“Starlink, we will diversify away from, no question,” Mr. Carney said, referring to the American-based cluster of communication satellites, run by Elon Musk’s SpaceX, that have revolutionized the industry. He alluded to past disruptions and to Mr. Musk’s reluctance to provide Ukraine with data that would enable it to target parts of Crimea and Russia.

He acknowledged that other satellite network options are still less capable and resilient, but added that “from a defense perspective, and certainly pooled with other partners, Europeans, Koreans potentially, you get to scale and you cut that dependency.”

The Canadian government is reviewing a planned order of 88 Lockheed Martin F-35 jets and is also considering a counterproposal to acquire Swedish Saab Gripen fighters. Mr. Carney did not specify where he was on that decision, but he did say that he wanted to use Canada’s newly bolstered defense budget to order aircraft that perform well in the Arctic.

“It is a real decision because of differing capabilities, because of strategic dependencies, and because of the economic return,” he said.

Mr. Carney on Wednesday also reiterated his long-held view that a global financial system wholly dependent on the U.S. dollar was unsustainable. A move to a multipolar system in which there are several reserve currencies would “provide more flexibility,” he said.

He acknowledged that there was a “directional shift” underway in which countries were re-evaluating their exposure to the U.S. dollar, but he conceded that any pivot would be limited until there was “proper liberalization” of China’s currency and financial system. Still, Mr. Carney said he expected the demand for U.S. dollar alternatives to grow, in part because of the Trump administration’s decision to rewire trading relations and use integration as “leverage.”

“It’s the ‘fool me once, fool me twice’ point,” Mr. Carney said. “Once you see that, then you start to think, how do I diversify away?”

item.title: Trump Aides Seek to Jump Start Diplomacy With Iran as Crisis Widens
item.description:
Secretary of State Marco Rubio said on Wednesday that U.S. negotiators had tried to jump start diplomacy with Iran on its nuclear program through talks on the side of a United Nations summit the previous day.

The flurry of diplomacy came as Iran’s partners, the Houthis, pressed forward with their offensive in the region, as a second front widened in a conflict that began when the United States and Israel attacked Iran in February.

Mr. Rubio said that the Americans involved in the talks, Steve Witkoff and Jared Kushner, were carrying out President Trump’s orders to continue a dialogue with Iran that prioritized persuading the country to end nuclear development involving enriching uranium.

Mr. Rubio added that Iran’s control of the Strait of Hormuz, which occurred as a result of the war, must also be addressed.

Mr. Witkoff is a special envoy for Mr. Trump, while Mr. Kushner is a businessman who is the president’s son-in-law and has no government position.

“If there’s an opportunity to exchange ideas and messages, we will,” Mr. Rubio told reporters in a news conference at a hotel in New York. “And that’s what largely yesterday was. It was positive in that regard.”

But ultimately, he said, “I don’t want to mischaracterize this as a major breakthrough. But at the same time, I think it was significant that at least there was a conversation.”

On Tuesday, Mr. Trump threatened to “annihilate the Islamic republic” if a deal to end the war was not reached.

The hourslong meeting between Mr. Witkoff and Mr. Kushner on one side and Abbas Araghchi, Iran’s foreign minister, on the other was mediated by Qatar, which has often acted as an interlocutor among the hostile parties.

Mr. Rubio said the information he has received about on the meeting is that “basically it was a continuation of conversations that have occurred in the past with people involved in those conversations.”

Mr. Rubio expressed skepticism that some of Iran’s hard-line leaders, ones who embrace the legacy of revolution, as he put it, would commit to deals that negotiators reached with the Americans.

An arm of Iran’s military, the Islamic Revolutionary Guards Corps, consolidated power after a top tier of the country’s leadership was killed in an initial strike in the war. That military unit sees itself as a guardian of the 1979 Islamic revolution in Iran.

“The ultimate decision making in Iran lies in the hands of people that are strong believers in Iran the revolution,” Mr. Rubio said. “And that makes interactions problematic.”

On Wednesday, the spokesman for Iran’s foreign ministry, Esmail Baghaei, who is also in New York, said Iran laid out its conditions for reviving diplomacy, which included ending a U.S. naval blockade, releasing the country’s frozen assets and ending hostilities on all fronts.

Those demands were enshrined in a 14-point peace agreement that the United States and Iran signed in June, a document commonly called a memorandum of understanding. The agreement eroded after Iranian hard-liners attacked commercial ships crossing the Strait for Hormuz. The U.S. military has been trying to ensure that ships can safely cross the waterway along its southern half, which is nearer to Oman than to Iran.

Mr. Rubio reiterated that Iran had violated the agreement. Mr. Trump has backed away from it and said he wants a more robust deal.

“What the meeting didn’t produce is a way to bridge the gap between two sides that believe they have more leverage than, and can outlast, the other” said Robert Malley, who was a top Iran negotiator in the Obama and Biden administrations.

The Houthi offensive in the region, to counter Saudi Arabia, has created a bigger crisis. The Yemeni group has seized control of another crucial waterway for international commercial shipping, the Bab al-Mandab Strait. The Houthis control most of Yemen and have armed insurgent units that withstood years of attacks by a Saudi-led military force starting in 2015, and also endured a U.S. bombing campaign last year.

Officials in the region fear that Iran could try to persuade the Houthis to further restrict commercial shipping in that waterway, which would add to the turmoil in the global economy. The U.S.-Israeli war has already sent the price of crude oil soaring, and consumers around the world have been complaining.

On Wednesday, in a speech at the United Nations, Iran’s president, Masoud Pezeshkian, vowed to defy the United States, but also expressed openness to negotiations.

“Iran must be understood by Mr. Trump and those who seek to bully us that we are ready for dialogue and diplomacy and negotiations without accepting the language of force,” he said.

When a reporter asked whether Mr. Trump might seek help from Xi Jinping, the leader of China, during a state visit in Washington this week to get Iran to agree to a settlement to the war, Mr. Rubio said, “I think the president will raise every relevant topic that involves the world.” He declined to discuss further details of the planned talks

Mr. Rubio was also asked why Mr. Trump did not just declare victory and walk away from the war now that the U.S. military had managed to seal off Iranian nuclear sites with rubble by bombing those sites in June 2025.

“Because at the end of the day you have to have not simply the destruction of facilities, you have to have a long-term and enforceable commitment to never pursue a nuclear weapon, ever,” Mr. Rubio said. “As long as they’re governed by the people they have now, that’s an unacceptable risk to the world.”

Michael Crowley and Farnaz Fassihi contributed reporting.

item.title: Families Urge Trump to Press Xi to Free Detained Americans
item.description:
The families of two Americans who have been listed by the U.S. government as wrongfully detained in China are urging President Trump to press President Xi Jinping for their release when the two leaders meet this week.

One of the Americans is Youlin Chen, a seismologist who was detained by Chinese state security officers and accused of spying while he was visiting relatives in Beijing in 2024. Mr. Chen, who was born in China, has conducted research for U.S. government and military agencies, including on the use of seismological data to better detect and analyze possible nuclear tests in North Korea. His family and colleagues say he has not done anything illegal.

The other detainee is U Min Zin, who was arrested in June while visiting southwest China to attend a conference at the invitation of the Chinese government. Mr. Min Zin is the executive director of a policy research group that focuses on Myanmar, where he was born and became a student activist in the pro-democracy movement.

Yufang Rong, the wife of Mr. Chen, said in an emailed statement that she met officials from the State Department and the National Security Council this week and that they told her that Mr. Trump would discuss both men with Mr. Xi.

Mr. Min Zin’s wife, Sylvia Zin, told a House of Representatives foreign affairs subcommittee hearing last week that she was “deeply hopeful” that Mr. Trump would advocate for her husband’s release.

“Over a hundred days into his detention, my husband has not been granted access to his Chinese lawyers, and I have no idea where he is being held,” she said. “I’m trying to be strong for our daughter, but I’m constantly wondering if he’s OK and how to get him back home to us.”

The State Department, which earlier officially declared Mr. Chen and Mr. Min Zin wrongfully detained, did not immediately respond to a request for comment. The U.S. government is obligated to treat those designated wrongfully detained abroad as hostages of a foreign government, and to work to seek their release.

It is unclear how Mr. Trump will raise the detentions with Mr. Xi. The Chinese government often shrugs off American pressure to release detainees and prisoners. But personal intervention from the U.S. president may help win a quicker release for Mr. Chen and Mr. Min Zin, said John Kamm, founder of the Dui Hua Foundation, a San Francisco-based group that works for the release of dissidents, rights activists and political prisoners in China.

“If Trump asks Xi to do him a personal favor by releasing these two citizens, the chances are good that Xi will accommodate his request,” Mr. Kamm said.

In July, China released the pastor of a prominent underground church in China who was detained last year, less than two months after Mr. Trump raised his case with Mr. Xi during talks in Beijing.

Supporters of Jimmy Lai, a pro-democracy businessman, have also called on Mr. Trump to use his leverage with the Chinese leader to win freedom for the dissident. Mr. Lai, a Chinese-born British citizen, was sentenced in February to 20 years in prison in Hong Kong on political charges, including “conspiracy to collude with foreign forces.” His imprisonment has attracted widespread condemnation in Washington and in Britain.

item.title: U.K. Far-Right Activist Is Arrested After Slashing Dinghy in English Channel
item.description:
A far-right activist known for organizing anti-immigrant rallies in Britain was arrested on Wednesday after he shared a video of himself slashing an inflatable dinghy in the English Channel while a person was on board.

A British police force, the Hampshire and Isle of Wight Constabulary, said in a statement that it had arrested a 37-year-old man. It did not further identify him, in line with British policing rules on not naming suspects who have not been charged.

But the man, Daniel Thomas, streamed a video on YouTube on Wednesday evening that appeared to show the arrest, at a gas station.

In a statement on Thursday, the police force said it had arrested the man on suspicion of several crimes, including destroying a ship or endangering its safety, and of criminal damage with intent to endanger life.

The arrest came after Mr. Thomas, who uses the name Danny Tommo, shared a video of himself in the English Channel pursuing a boat carrying migrants from France to Britain.

Mr. Thomas has espoused extremist views against migration and urged his followers to rally at ports and other sites housing newly arrived asylum seekers. In 2016, he was sentenced to two years in custody for an attempted kidnapping.

In June, Mr. Thomas said he had started a group, Patriot Platform, to channel anti-migration sentiment. He has claimed credit for recruiting protesters to gather recently in Dover and Portsmouth, where hundreds of masked men dressed in black blocked roads and chanted “Stop the boats!”

This month, Britain’s home secretary, Shabana Mahmood, described Mr. Thomas as an “outright racist.”

In the video filmed at sea, Mr. Thomas could be heard saying, “You’re on English territory. This is England,” before slashing the dinghy with a blade. No migrants were on the boat, but an emergency responder was aboard.

“You’ve got time to get off the boat,” Mr. Thomas shouted at the worker.

The Royal National Lifeboat Institution, a charity that dispatches rescue vessels, said that two of its lifeboats had been sent on Tuesday to assist a small boat. The charity did not say where the boat had come from but that it had been at sea for 36 hours. British Border Force vessels had not initially been able to help, the charity said.

The French coast guard said in a statement that a boat carrying about 60 migrants had crossed the English Channel.

Britain’s Home Office, which oversees immigration enforcement, said that border officials were investigating the episode. A small boat disembarked on the coast of Dover on Tuesday afternoon, the office said, and 21 people had been detained and taken to a migrant facility for processing.

The police said in its statement on Thursday that the 37 year-old man remained in custody.

Mr. Thomas is a close associate of the far-right activist Stephen Yaxley-Lennon, widely known as Tommy Robinson, who shared an appeal on social media on Thursday in support of him.

Three other people were also charged after anti-immigrant demonstrators on Tuesday gathered in Gosport, a town on the south coast of England, to protest the boat crossings. Six people were arrested, and three people were charged with assaulting an emergency worker.

item.title: Abbas Presses Case for Palestinian State in Taped General Assembly Address
item.description:
The Palestinian leader Mahmoud Abbas renewed his call for a two-state solution in a videotaped address to the General Assembly on Thursday, as he accused Israel of prosecuting “a genocidal war” against Palestinians “that has created an unprecedented humanitarian catastrophe.”

For the second year in a row, Mr. Abbas, 90, did not appear in person at the annual gathering because the Trump administration denied him a visa to travel to New York. The General Assembly requires all world leaders who give speeches to the body to show up at United Nations headquarters in New York for the event. But it can make an exception under extreme circumstances, and the U.N.’s 193 members voted last week, as they did last year, to allow Mr. Abbas to send a videotaped speech.

Mr. Abbas, who the president of the Palestinian Authority, forcefully renewed calls for the creation of an independent Palestinian state, one that he said would exist peacefully alongside the state of Israel.

“We seek a democratic Palestinian state that respects the rule of law and human rights, a non-militarized state that lives in security and peace alongside the state of Israel,” Mr. Abbas said. “It is possible.”

Palestinian statehood has widespread support at the U.N., with 157 out of 193 member states recognizing Palestine as an independent state. In 2025, some major Western countries, including France, Britain, Canada, Australia and Portugal, formally recognized a Palestinian state at a conference on the sidelines of the General Assembly.

Mr. Abbas condemned the persistent Israeli violence toward Palestinian civilians in Gaza and the occupied West Bank. Israel’s annexations of land in the West Bank for Jewish settlements have been heavily criticized as an impediment to the creation of a Palestinian state.

He characterized the continued Israeli attacks in Gaza and settler violence in the West Bank as “a malicious colonial scheme aimed at making the lives of Palestinians more difficult in their homeland and forcing them to leave it.”

Israel has rejected those accusations, justifying its conduct in Gaza as an attempt to root out terrorism by Hamas that it says threatens its national security. The Israeli prime minister, Benjamin Netanyahu, 76, is expected to address the General Assembly on Thursday afternoon.

The conflict in Gaza is in its fourth year. Israeli attacks have continued despite a cease-fire brokered by the United States, and Hamas, the militant group that once controlled the enclave, has not been disarmed. Much of the enclave lies in ruins, and reconstruction efforts are suspended.

In the West Bank, extremist Israeli settlers are still attacking Palestinians and have in some instances taken over their land by force. The Israeli government also has expanded the building of new settlements even though they have been deemed illegal under international law.

Mr. Abbas welcomed President Trump’s Board of Peace plan for Gaza, which U.N. Security Council adopted in a resolution, as a blueprint for ending the war, disarming Hamas and rebuilding the enclave its shattered infrastructure. That plan has since stalled.

“Regretfully, we have not seen any of this materialize on the ground,” Mr. Abbas said.

The Palestinian leader rejected the notion that Palestinians would ever voluntarily leave their land. Israel has been accused of pursuing policies in Gaza that make life for Palestinians impossible by destroying their homes, schools, universities, hospitals and infrastructure.

“We will not leave our homeland,” Mr. Abbas said. “We will not accept resettlement. We will not allow anyone to decide for us.”

item.title: China Plans to Send More Pandas to the U.S., Making Life Bearable for Fans
item.description:
The pandas are coming!

That promise from Xi Jinping, China’s leader, could end up being regarded by many Americans as the most positive diplomatic outcome of his state visit to Washington this week.

While meeting with President Trump, Mr. Xi announced on Thursday morning that China would soon send two pandas to Zoo Atlanta. The zoo is one of a handful of institutions in the United States that has paid to host pandas on loan from China over the last half-century.

Mr. Xi called the black-and-white fur balls “envoys of friendship” — an icon of literal soft diplomacy.

Zoo Atlanta sent a family of pandas back to China in October 2024, and since then it has been in talks with Chinese conservation officials to get another pair. Zoo officials announced in August that they had reached a new research agreement with the China Wildlife Conservation Association, one of two groups in China that do scientific studies on pandas, promote their breeding and arrange to lend them to overseas institutions.

That announcement in August opened the way for the Chinese group to organize the shipping to Atlanta of two pandas, Ping Ping (male) and Fu Shuang (female). Mr. Xi’s declaration confirmed that would happen soon.

U.S.-China relations are a roller coaster, and tensions have been high for the last decade. American officials accuse China of unfair trade practices and supporting adversaries of the United States, and the governments clash over the U.S. naval presence and Chinese military activity around Taiwan and in the greater Pacific region. But panda diplomacy abides.

That began during President Richard M. Nixon’s landmark visit to Beijing in 1972, when the first lady, Pat Nixon, mentioned her fondness for pandas — “I love them” — to China’s premier, Zhou Enlai. Within two months, China had sent a female and a male panda, Ling-Ling and Hsing-Hsing, to the National Zoo in Washington.

The zoo paid $1 million per year to host them, a fee that dropped to $500,000 after the first decade. Other zoos jumped on board, including in Atlanta, San Diego and Memphis.

However, two years ago, it looked like a surge in U.S.-China tensions might be jeopardizing the diplomacy. For the first time in decades, there were no pandas in the United States — all of them had been returned to China at the request of the conservation groups there, with the final two families leaving the National Zoo in 2023 and Zoo Atlanta the next year.

Many people speculated that the rocky geopolitical relations had prompted China’s move.

But some zoo officials said the Chinese groups had asked for the pandas back because of where they were in their life cycles. Pandas are notoriously unenthusiastic about sex, and any pandas born overseas — a cause for celebration — are sent back to China to be raised in conservation parks in Sichuan Province. When they reach a certain age, the parents are usually sent back as well. (A New York Times investigation in 2024 raised questions about the breeding and expensive loan program run from China.)

In November 2023, during a visit to San Francisco just one week after the National Zoo had sent back its three pandas, Mr. Xi said China might send more pandas to the United States soon.

“I was told that many American people, especially children, were really reluctant to say goodbye to the pandas and went to the zoo to see them off,” he said at the time.

Yun Chuan and Xin Bao arrived at the San Diego Zoo in June 2024. And that October, Bao Li and Qing Bao, both age 3, arrived at the National Zoo, ending an 11-month absence there.

Now Zoo Atlanta will get its pair, if Mr. Xi keeps his word. The question is whether panda huggers will be able to bear the wait.

item.title: In Trumpeting His Ballroom Project, Trump Has Used China as an Example
item.description:
President Trump showed off some of the construction that he’s had done at the White House to President Xi Jinping of China during their summit on Thursday, and Mr. Trump had reasons to want the Chinese leader’s nod of approval.

Throughout the uproar over Mr. Trump’s demolition of the East Wing and construction of a grandiose ballroom on the site, the American president has repeatedly cited the Great Hall of the People in China as inspiration and competition with his own design.

On the first full day of Mr. Xi’s visit, Mr. Trump gave him a brief tour of the ballroom construction site, as well as the helipad project that was officially opened this week. Mr. Trump called the Chinese leader “an expert on stone” who “loves good granite” as Mr. Xi stood by without changing his expression.

The Great Hall looms over Tiananmen Square in central Beijing, and it hosts the annual meeting of China’s Communist Party-run legislature. Chinese leaders also meet visiting foreign leaders in its halls, including Mr. Trump in May and in 2017.

On that visit in May, members of Mr. Trump’s delegation, including Secretary of State Marco Rubio, marveled at the size and splendor of the Great Hall. They were echoing Mr. Trump’s own admiration for the building, which covers over 1.8 million square feet across four levels, and its central auditorium can seat about 10,000 people. (Mr. Trump’s planned ballroom covers 90,000 square feet.)

“So we’re building something that’s going to be the most beautiful anywhere in the world,” Mr. Trump said at a Republican midterm convention in Dallas earlier this month. “When I was in China, they have a building — it’s called the Great Hall of China. It’s a serious hall. This is a very large hall, but we’re going to top it, you know?”

Mr. Trump has described his admiration for the Great Hall on at least six occasions in recent months, according to a review of his speeches and news conferences. “They have a very large ballroom, beautiful ballroom,” Mr. Trump said in the Rose Garden of the White House in July. “We don’t have that, but we’re going to have one that tops everything.”

The grandeur of the Great Hall reflected the ambitions of Mao Zedong, the autocratic leader who ordered its construction. China “must build a grand hall that can hold 10,000 people,” Mao said in 1945, when he was still leading revolutionary forces from caves in rural China.

The Great Hall was built in less than a year starting in late 1958, during Mao’s fervent, and ultimately calamitous, Great Leap Forward: his attempt to rapidly industrialize China. By many scholars’ estimates, 20 million or more people died in the famine caused by Mao’s policies.

item.title: A Spirited Battle Over Data Centers
item.description:
Energy prices are rising. Demand for electricity is surging. Next year is expected to be the hottest on record as a severe El Niño weather pattern gathers steam. And there is no consensus about how the political world or the private sector should meet this moment.

Those were some of the themes that defined a series of expansive conversations we had with policymakers, business leaders and activists yesterday at the Climate Forward live event that we hosted at the Times Center in New York City. (You can watch videos from the sessions here.)

The data centers roiling the nation and shaking up the midterm elections emerged as the day’s main battleground.

During the first panel of the day, I spoke with the environmental activist Erin Brockovich, whose work was the basis of the 2000 movie bearing her name, and State Representative Justin J. Pearson of Tennessee, both of whom are working to oppose data center projects.

Pearson, a Democrat who is currently campaigning to represent Tennessee’s Ninth Congressional District, drew attention to the health effects of air pollution from data centers, citing estimates that additional pollution from gas turbines and diesel generators could kill dozens of people each year.

For Pearson, the potential effects of data centers are quite real. “It’s killing people in communities now,” he said of air pollution. He also accused Elon Musk of illegally installing natural gas turbines near his community in Memphis.

(Watch the conversation with Brockovich and Pearson here.)

The sites near his district have drawn scrutiny since the N.A.A.C.P. sued Musk’s xAI in June, saying that the company has been operating natural-gas-burning turbines without the proper permits.

Brockovich recently started a data center mapping project to crowdsource new developments nationwide, and criticized the secrecy of deals with local governments.

“Nondisclosure agreements. Secrecies. Not being informed. And just all of a sudden, things were being rezoned,” she said, describing what she is hearing from local communities. “They didn’t have a vote. They didn’t have a say. And that has really set them off.”

Later in the day I interviewed Gov. Abigail Spanberger of Virginia, a Democrat. Her state has the most data centers in the country. Loudoun County alone has more than 250, which have brought in huge tax revenues but also sparked an intense backlash from neighbors.

Spanberger told me that states should do more to regulate data centers and address their effects on air and noise pollution, energy prices and surrounding communities, and explained the rationale behind a set of policies she announced last week aimed at putting guardrails on the industry.

“While ultimately the decision needs to live with the locality, as they’re balancing what they’re choosing to approve or not approve, the state has a role in creating the real rules of the road,” she said.

(Watch the conversation with Gov. Spanberger here.)

Spanberger called for limiting the amount of electricity that data centers can generate from natural gas and incentivizing developers to supply their own clean energy. But she stopped short of endorsing the one-year moratorium on data center construction issued by Gov. Kathy Hochul of New York, who is also a Democrat.

We also heard from the data center industry and its allies in the White House.

Josh Parker, head of sustainability at the chipmaker Nvidia, told my colleague Cecilia Kang that artificial intelligence has “huge potential to drive net emissions reductions.”

The data center boom has pushed U.S. electricity demand upward for the first time in decades, fueling the construction of natural gas turbines and diesel generators that will increase greenhouse gas emissions.

But Parker said artificial-intelligence-driven energy savings in manufacturing, buildings and transportation could help cancel out the technology’s carbon footprint, as can “moonshots,” like nuclear fusion.

“Even if A.I. only accelerates commercializable nuclear fusion or even advanced fission by a year, the terms of carbon savings and energy abundance and affordability are really, really dramatic,” he said.

Instead of just considering the technology industry’s direct emissions, Mr. Parker said, “what’s really important is what is the net impact of the technology,” after accounting for future energy savings in other sectors.

And at the end of a wide-ranging interview, Energy Secretary Chris Wright told me that he supported communities right to decide whether or not they want data center as a neighbor.

“Communities should choose,” he said. “We’re not imposing data centers on anyone. We’re saying look at the trade-offs. The positives may be much bigger than the negatives.”

Wright, a former fossil fuel executive, likened the swelling backlash against data centers to the movement to curb hydraulic fracturing, or fracking.

(Watch the conversation with Sec. Wright here.)

“The opposition to data centers, a lot of it is very hyped,” he said. “It’s like anti-fracking.” Wright added that critics say “it’s going to ruin your water. It’s going to drive up your prices and pollute your thing.” But, he argued, “it’s easy to scare people. It’s harder to reassure people.”

Despite President Trump’s enthusiastic support for the industry, public opposition to data centers has rapidly gained momentum in recent months amid concerns about the rising costs of electricity, skepticism about the societal benefits of A.I. and anxieties about their environmental effects. New York became the first state to issue a yearlong moratorium on new construction in July, and the issue has become a point of contention in the upcoming midterm elections.

Pearson repeated calls for a national moratorium on data center construction. “If these things were so good, they would be being built at Mar-a-Lago,” he said.

“It’s the billionaires versus the rest of us,” Pearson said.

Claire Brown and Maxine Joselow contributed reporting.

In their words

Those are the words of Keith Parker, a senior fisheries biologist and member of the Yurok Tribe, which led the decades-long campaign to have dams of the Klamath River removed.

The river, which flows through Oregon and California, has been cleared of big barriers for the first time in more than a century after the largest dam removal project in American history. And, now, Rebecca Dzombak reports, a new study shows the river is experiencing a significant rebound of native chinook salmon. After years of contentious debate and careful planning, the last of four dams was removed in 2024.

The return of the salmon has already had an effect on local life, she writes: “Some tribes, including the Yurok, are already reaping the benefits of stronger fall chinook runs. The Yurok in August held their annual salmon festival; for the first time in years, they actually served salmon. They’re also distributing salmon to elders and schools.”

Read the full article.

climate law

A second federal judge in New York has ruled that the state’s new climate “superfund” law is unconstitutional, dealing a blow to the nascent effort to popularize such measures around the country. The decision on Wednesday came from a challenge by the Justice Department and the Environmental Protection Agency.

The groundbreaking law would require fossil fuel companies to pay billions of dollars to cover the costs of climate change. Vermont and New York are the only states to have passed climate superfund laws, but they have been proposed in several other states. A legal challenge to Vermont’s law is also pending.

The plaintiffs in the cases have argued that the laws illegally encroach on the role of the federal government and its ability to balance environmental, energy and economic considerations. Republicans and the energy industry have vigorously opposed the proposed laws. — Karen Zraick

Read the full article.

Related: Republicans Seek Protections for Oil Giants Against Climate Lawsuits

In case you missed it

Less than a year ago, Gov. Greg Abbott of Texas welcomed data centers and the state was poised to become an epicenter of the boom. But, now Abbott, a Republican running for re-election, is effectively halting the development of new data centers in the state.

A group of civil-rights and free-speech lawyers said that they had identified “staggering” missteps in a $345 million verdict against Greenpeace last year and argued that the judgment should be overturned.

A federal judge has dismissed a novel lawsuit filed by Michigan’s attorney general, a Democrat. The suit accused fossil fuel companies of creating a “cartel” and colluding to raise costs for residents by suppressing the development of renewable energy and concealing information about the risks of global warming.

One last thing

Matthew Haag spoke to school districts that have introduced electric buses, fueled in part by $2.4 billion federal grants from the Biden administration.But, he reports, the “rollout has been rocky, rife with technical challenges and logistical headaches — and resistance from voters.” One school district in New York spent $1 million to electrify two buses. Other area have reported battery ranges that are low to handle some bus routes and repeated mechanical problems.

Read the full article.

Related: A Brand-New Electric Bus, No Charge. (That Was One Problem.)

Germany, which is Europe’s biggest economy, has pledged to phase out fossil fuels by 2045, The Guardian reports.

Inside Climate News reports that scientists have estimated that more than 450,000 people are likely to die in the next six months from the additional heat the strong El Niño weather

item.title: Netanyahu Attacks Mamdani in Heated U.N. Speech
item.description:
Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu of Israel again attacked Mayor Zohran Mamdani during a speech to the U.N. General Assembly on Thursday, accusing the mayor of antisemitism and saying his criticism of Israel had endangered New York’s Jewish population.

Mr. Netanyahu said that since Mr. Mamdani took office, “many Jews no longer feel safe in New York.”

Mr. Mamdani, New York’s first Muslim mayor, has long been an outspoken critic of Israel’s treatment of Palestinians and has denounced Mr. Netanyahu as a war criminal. Mr. Netanyahu has repeatedly assailed the mayor over his views, and many of the claims the prime minister made during his speech echoed his past attacks on Mr. Mamdani.

Over several minutes, Mr. Netanyahu took particular aim at Mr. Mamdani’s assertion that Israel’s conduct of the war in Gaza amounted to genocide.

A United Nations commission, as well as international and Israeli human rights groups, have concluded that Israel committed genocide in Gaza during the war there, which was sparked by the deadly Hamas-led terrorist attacks on Israel on Oct. 7, 2023.

Mr. Netanyahu has vigorously rejected those claims, and in his speech on Thursday said that “accusing Israel of genocide is the greatest lie of the century.”

He also mentioned Mr. Mamdani’s wife, Rama Duwaji, who has been criticized for liking social media posts supporting the Palestinian cause immediately after the Oct. 7 attacks.

In response to Mr. Netanyahu, Mr. Mamdani accused the prime minister of using his U.N. speech “to repeat baseless lies meant to sanitize his genocide of Palestinians.”

“Yet no lie can change the fact that he remains the subject of an International Criminal Court arrest warrant alleging war crimes and crimes against humanity,” the mayor said in a statement.

Mr. Mamdani did not attend Mr. Netanyahu’s speech. While it was taking place, he was scheduled to join the prime minister of the Netherlands for “a discussion with L.G.B.T.Q.+ youth.”

Shortly before the speech began, Mr. Mamdani posted a wordless, one-minute video on social media that showed him planting an olive tree at Gracie Mansion, his official residence, and eating dinner with Palestinian families from Gaza.

“May peace be our future,” the mayor wrote in a caption.

Mr. Mamdani’s stance on Israel has made him a potent political foil for the prime minister, who is in the midst of a critical re-election campaign. Mr. Netanyahu’s Likud party has put Mr. Mamdani’s face on billboards and campaign posters in Israel, alongside images of the leaders of Iran, Turkey and Hezbollah.

Earlier this month, the prime minister posted an A.I.-generated campaign video that portrayed the mayor celebrating at the prospect of Mr. Netanyahu’s electoral defeat alongside President Recep Tayyip Erdogan of Turkey, Ayatollah Mojtaba Khamenei of Iran and President Mahmoud Abbas of the Palestinian Authority.

Earlier this week, Mr. Netanyahu released a video broadside against the mayor, falsely accusing him of supporting Hamas and inciting anti-Jewish riots in New York.

Mr. Mamdani vowed during last year’s mayoral campaign to execute an international warrant for Mr. Netanyahu’s arrest the next time the prime minister visited New York. Mr. Netanyahu was accused of war crimes in 2024 by the International Criminal Court; he has denied the charges.

Mr. Mamdani backed off on his pledge in July, acknowledging in a video that the city does not have legal authority to make the arrest, but he urged the federal government to do so. In a Fox News appearance after the video was posted, Mr. Netanyahu accused the mayor of “fomenting hate.”

The mayor has condemned Hamas as a terrorist organization and described the Oct. 7 attacks as “a horrific war crime.” And while there has been an increase in antisemitic hate crimes in New York in recent years, as well as anti-Israel protests that have sometimes turned chaotic, there have been no riots targeting Jews during Mr. Mamdani’s time in public office.

In the first week of Mr. Mamdani’s term, the government of Israel accused him of antisemitism after he revoked two executive orders signed by his predecessor, Eric Adams, which barred city agencies from boycotting Israel and defined some criticism of Israel as antisemitic. Mr. Mamdani said at the time that “protecting Jewish New Yorkers is going to be a focus of my administration.”

Mr. Mamdani’s continued criticism of Israel has nevertheless alienated or unsettled many Jewish New Yorkers and has drawn warnings from Jewish leaders who believe his commentary inflames antisemitism. But progressive Jewish groups that support the mayor have praised his positions.

When Mr. Mamdani admitted that the city could not arrest Mr. Netanyahu, he all but encouraged protests against the prime minister, prompting questions about whether he might make an appearance at any of the demonstrations planned to coincide with Mr. Netanyahu’s speech on Thursday afternoon. The mayor opted not to attend any protests ahead of the speech.

item.title: Amid Protests, Netanyahu Castigates Foes and Mayor of New York City
item.description:
Fighting for his political life back home, Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu of Israel gave a pugnacious address at the United Nations General Assembly on Thursday, casting his nation as falsely accused of genocide and his people as indomitable fighters against terrorism and antisemitism.

At times pounding the lectern and raising his voice, Mr. Netanyahu took aim at Israel’s military enemies like Iran, Hezbollah, Hamas and their allied forces in Yemen and Iraq. But he also assailed Mayor Zohran Mamdani of New York City, President Recep Tayyip Erdogan of Turkey and Western European leaders he said had “chosen to succumb to the antisemitic mob.”

As the Israeli leader took the podium, many of the international diplomats filed out of the hall, as they have in the past, but his speech seemed tuned far more to a domestic audience than an international one.

Israel will hold a general election next month, and Mr. Netanyahu, trailing in the polls, is trying to rally support with a defiant message that international criticism of Israel is not only wrong, but also dishonest and immoral, and that the nation is besieged by immense threats that only he can vanquish.

On Thursday, he cast the war that he and President Trump launched against Iran seven months ago in the most dire, but also hyperbolic, terms, saying that Iran must be prevented from developing nuclear weapons.

“It’s one of the easiest decisions I’ve had to make as prime minister, because if we hadn’t done it, we’d all be dead,” he said of the attacks on Iran. He added, “Israel and America acted together, not only to protect ourselves, but to save civilization.”

Israel’s longest-serving prime minister, Mr. Netanyahu has warned for decades that Iran was close to developing nuclear weapons. But it was only in Mr. Trump’s current term that he managed to persuade a U.S. leader to join in military action to prevent it. The close relationship between the two men has cooled as the war has dragged on.

Mr. Netanyahu recounted the Oct. 7, 2023, Hamas-led attack that officials said killed about 1,200 people in Israel and led to the taking of about 250 hostages to Gaza, violence, he said, that had been carried out “with fiendish glee, with sadistic joy.”

“We didn’t collapse,” he said. “We rose and fought like lions.”

In the ensuing Israeli military attacks in Gaza, more than 70,000 people were killed, officials said, and much of the enclave was reduced to rubble, leading to international accusations, including by a U.N. commission, that Israel was committing genocide. Mr. Netanyahu denounced that charge as “the greatest lie of the century” and claimed that Israel had “the most moral army in the world.”

He also lashed out at Mr. Mamdani, who has called on the federal government to execute an arrest warrant on Mr. Netanyahu from the International Criminal Court. Mr. Mamdani’s criticism of Israel has alienated some Jewish New Yorkers, though others — particularly young progressives — still support him. Mr. Netanyahu called Mr. Mamdani antisemitic, a label the mayor rejects.

“Mr. Mamdani, since you were elected mayor of this city, many Jews no longer feel safe in New York,” Mr. Netanyahu said.

Minutes before the speech, Mr. Mamdani released a wordless video that showed him planting an olive tree at Gracie Mansion and eating dinner with Palestinian families from Gaza. “May peace be our future,” he said in a caption on X.

Mr. Netanyahu cast Israeli settlers in the occupied West Bank, whose presence much of the world considers an illegal encroachment into land destined for a Palestinian state, as mostly peaceful neighbors and victims of Palestinian violence. He scoffed at the concept of settler violence against Palestinians, though it has been well documented.

Palestinians in the West Bank “shoot at pregnant women, they shoot entire families,” he said. “Of course, none of this is covered in the international press or in the social media, none of it. What they cover is a handful of young juvenile delinquents, about 150 in number, who go and throw stones, who chop down olive trees, occasionally they fire up, they lit some fires.”

The United Nations reported that 18 Palestinians were killed over the first seven months of this year in violence by extremist settlers, who are often heavily armed. Many more suffered injury and damaged property, the agency said, or were forced to abandon their homes.

item.title: Netanyahu, Addressing U.N., Denounces Israel’s Critics as ‘Moral Cowards’
item.description:
Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu of Israel gave a combative speech to the United Nations General Assembly on Thursday in which he defended the wars in Gaza and in Iran as a “battle against barbarians” and accused his country’s many critics of being hypocrites.

Directly addressing the protesters who were outside the building, he demanded to know where they had been when Iranian security forces killed thousands of people demonstrating against the regime in Tehran in January.

“Did you organize mass rallies, hunger strikes?” Mr. Netanyahu asked. “Did you protest outside the Iranian mission to the U. N.? Did you speak out, for that matter, for Christians persecuted in Iran and throughout the Middle East? No, no, you didn’t do that. Because you’re phony human rights protesters.”

Mr. Netanyahu also directly criticized Mayor Zohran Mamdani of New York, the city’s first Muslim leader, who has called Mr. Netanyahu a “war criminal” and at one time called for him to be arrested.

“To all those spreading these lies about my country and about our brave soldiers, whether they sit in this hall or in the office of the antisemitic mayor of New York, I say this: Shame on you!” Mr. Netanyahu said. “Shame on you for distorting the facts. Shame on you for inverting victim and aggressor. Shame on you for spitting in the face of truth.”

Mr. Netanyahu addressed the General Assembly just hours after the Palestinian leader, Mahmoud Abbas, delivered a recorded video address in which he condemned Israeli actions in Gaza and the West Bank as “a malicious colonial scheme” aimed at forcing Palestinians to leave their homeland. He urged world leaders to restrain Israel and “ensure the viability of the two-state solution.”

“We seek a democratic Palestinian state that respects the rule of law and human rights, a non-militarized state that lives in security and peace alongside the state of Israel,” Mr. Abbas said. “It is possible.”

The dueling speeches cast into stark relief the sharp divisions in the Israeli-Palestinian conflict, as well as Israel’s increasing isolation on the world stage.

Mr. Abbas, the leader of the Palestine Liberation Organization and the Palestinian Authority, did not appear in person because, for the second year in a row, the Trump administration refused to grant him a visa to travel to New York.

The State Department accused Palestinian officials of trying to “internationalize the Israeli-Palestinian conflict,” including by seeking to bring cases to international tribunals. In response, the U.N.’s 193 members voted last week, as they did last year, to allow Mr. Abbas to send a videotaped speech.

When Mr. Netanyahu took the podium, he was greeted with boos, and many of the diplomats in the hall walked out, as they did last year. Supporters of the Israeli leader, meanwhile, began chanting, “Am Yisrael Chai,” a popular refrain meaning “the people of Israel live.”

“If there are any other moral cowards who haven’t yet left this hall, please do so now,” Mr. Netanyahu said.

At times pounding the lectern and raising his voice, Mr. Netanyahu took aim at those with whom Israel has clashed militarily: Iran, Hezbollah in Lebanon, Hamas in Gaza and their allied forces in Yemen and Iraq. But he also spent considerable time assailing Mayor Mamdani, President Recep Tayyip Erdogan of Turkey and Western European leaders who, he said, “have chosen to succumb to the antisemitic mob.”

In response to Mr. Netanyahu’s attacks, Mr. Mamdani accused the prime minister of using his U.N. speech “to repeat baseless lies meant to sanitize his genocide of Palestinians.”

“Yet no lie can change the fact that he remains the subject of an International Criminal Court arrest warrant alleging war crimes and crimes against humanity,” the mayor said.

Minutes before Mr. Netanyahu spoke, Mr. Mamdani released a wordless, minute-long video that showed him planting an olive tree at Gracie Mansion, the mayor’s official residence, and dining there with Palestinian families from Gaza.

“May peace be our future,” Mr. Mamdani wrote in a social media post accompanying the video.

Outside the United Nations, the police arrested protesters who were blocking an intersection at 39th Street and First Avenue, not far from the General Assembly hall, and chanting, “It is right to rebel; Netanyahu go to hell.” The protest was organized by Jewish Voice for Peace and attracted hundreds of demonstrators who wore shirts that read, “Fund people not bombs.”

Mr. Abbas assailed the Israeli military campaign in Gaza, calling it “a genocidal war that has created an unprecedented humanitarian catastrophe.” He also condemned Israel’s occupation of the West Bank, where he said settler attacks on Palestinians and the demolition of Palestinian homes, checkpoints and raids have been carried out under a policy of “racial discrimination, ethnic cleansing and state terrorism.”

“The danger is no longer limited to undermining the two-state solution and preventing the realization of the Palestinian state,” he said. “It has now come to threaten the very life and existence of the Palestinian people on their own land.”

Mr. Netanyahu cast Israeli settlers in the occupied West Bank, whose presence much of the world considers an illegal encroachment onto land destined for a Palestinian state, as mostly peaceful neighbors and victims of Palestinian violence.

He also rejected claims that Israel was carrying out a genocide in Gaza.

“What genocidal regime gives a million polio vaccinations to the enemy’s population?” he asked. “What genocidal regime enables the distribution of two million tons of food into Gaza? That’s a ton for every person. Accusing Israel of genocide is the greatest lie of the century.”

Mr. Netanyahu recounted the horror of Oct. 7, 2023, when a Hamas-led attack killed about 1,200 people in Israel and led to the abduction of about 250 hostages to Gaza, violence that he said had been carried out “with fiendish glee, with sadistic joy.”

“We didn’t collapse,” he said. “We rose and fought like lions.”

In the ensuing Israeli military attacks in Gaza, more than 70,000 people were killed, according to Gaza health officials, and much of the enclave was reduced to rubble, leading to international accusations, including by a U.N. commission, that Israel was committing genocide.

In 2024, the International Criminal Court issued an arrest warrant for Mr. Netanyahu and Israel’s former defense minister, Yoav Gallant, accusing them of crimes against humanity and war crimes in Gaza. The court also issued a warrant for a Hamas leader, Muhammad Deif. He was killed by an Israeli airstrike in Gaza.

Mr. Netanyahu is now facing a tough re-election campaign, and his political future is uncertain. His speech at the U.N., analysts said, was at least in part directed at the audience back home.

In his address, he cast the war that he and President Trump launched against Iran seven months ago, partly on the grounds that Iran must be prevented from developing nuclear weapons, in the most dire, existential terms.

“It’s one of the easiest decisions I’ve had to make as prime minister, because if we hadn’t done it, we’d all be dead,” he said. He added, “Israel and America acted together, not only to protect ourselves, but to save civilization.”

Mr. Netanyahu vowed that Israel would continue to fight against Iran and its allied militias in the Middle East “because we have no other choice.”

Reporting was contributed by Liam Stack, Miles G. Cohen and Richard Pérez-Peña.

item.title: Why the U.N. Still Matters
item.description:
A year ago, it felt as if the United Nations was on its last legs. It was running out of money, it seemed increasingly irrelevant and there was concern that Donald Trump would pull the United States out. There was even talk that his Board of Peace could become a sort of alternative, rival U.N.

But this week, as world leaders once again met in New York, there was a new energy. A.I. got its first-ever dedicated Security Council meeting. And Trump, though belligerent as ever, did what you’re meant to do at the U.N.: He engaged in diplomacy. But it’s hard to read the room from outside the building. So I spoke to my colleague Farnaz Fassihi, who has been inside U.N. headquarters all week.

Farnaz, I usually call you up to talk about Iran, but you’re also our U.N. bureau chief and have been covering these annual meetings for a decade. People love to discuss how irrelevant the U.N. has become. How much does the U.N. still matter?

It’s the only forum in the world that brings countries — all 193 of them — together under one roof. They call it the World Cup of diplomacy. Delegations attend bilateral meetings, group meetings, thematic meetings on things like rising ocean levels and food security. These are issues that need a space for discussion, and the U.N. is really the only place that offers that.

What comes out that’s actionable? Very little. But it moves the conversation forward. And there’s value to that if you believe in diplomacy. We’re so used to thinking, “Oh, the U.N. Security Council is so divided; the U.S. and China and Russia can’t agree on anything.” But as one U.N. expert pointed out, when you compare it to the Cold War days, when the U.S. and the Soviet Union were at loggerheads, the U.N. is still doing a lot more today than it was then.

What stood out to you this year?

Definitely artificial intelligence. A.I. went from a marginal issue to a big theme. The Security Council, which always picks what it sees as the most important issue for peace and stability, held a high-profile meeting on A.I., with Sam Altman and Dario Amodei, the bosses of OpenAI and Anthropic, briefing leaders.

For now, several of the countries that have veto power don’t seem very eager to act jointly. The U.S., China and Russia were essentially saying, “You can’t interfere in our sovereign decisions about technology.”

It was also the first time the head of a country actively at war with the U. S. has come to New York and addressed the U.N. How did that go down?

It was remarkable. In Afghanistan and Iraq, the U.S. toppled the governments so quickly that this situation was avoided. During the Vietnam War, Vietnam wasn’t yet a member state, so this was new — and a little surreal. Iran’s president, Masoud Pezeshkian, is getting Secret Service protection from the Americans.

People in Iran are pointing out the irony: Iranians are not safe in their own country, where America may attack and kill them. But in the U.S., they’re protected by the Secret Service and meeting with prime ministers and presidents. For Iran’s government that’s a symbolic win: We survived. We’re still standing.

How did Trump handle the situation?

It’s interesting. Last year, Trump just lashed out at countries and insulted the U.N. and people were nervous he’d pull the U.S. — the U.N.’s top funder — out altogether.

This year, from the U.N.’s perspective, at least, his speech was more measured. That might sound surprising, given that he talked about annihilating the Islamic republic and effectively threatened a war crime from the U.N. podium. But he was not threatening the U.N. itself. And in a way, he was doing what people do at the U.N. General Assembly: He used the platform to send a message.

Then, an hour later, we hear the Iranians and Americans have been meeting for two hours on the sidelines. Which is also what people do at U.N.G.A. though not usually after one party has just threatened to annihilate the other.

So, what I’m hearing you say is that the U.N. is still a useful talking shop. But perhaps no longer itself involved in conflict resolution?

The U.N.’s original and core mission was to prevent and mediate conflict, and that piece has slipped away. In Gaza, it had a very minimal role. In the Iran conflict, it’s had no voice. But it’s more than a talking shop. When it comes to humanitarian relief, for example, it’s really the only game in town. The response to floods in Nepal or earthquakes in Colombia and Venezuela, food aid in Gaza and Sudan, would not be possible without the U.N.’s staff, logistics, planes and regional hubs.

The secretary general, António Guterres, is leaving office in December. What should we expect next?

They’re looking for a new secretary general, but for now there’s no clear front runner. At every Security Council briefing I went to this week, they said they want someone who asserts themselves more on conflicts. They feel Guterres has been too passive. They think a new leader, possibly a woman for the first time, could energize the institution.

item.title: ‘All We Could See Was Red’: The Wildfires Choking Indonesian Borneo
item.description:
Staring out at the charred cemetery about 100 feet behind his house in Indonesian Borneo, Trovimus Akoi told of the sleepless Sunday night he spent battling an inferno far too close to home.

He first spotted the wildfire about half a mile away while feeding his chickens. Within hours, the fire tore across the parched terrain at terrifying speed. As the blaze closed in on his community, he and his neighbors armed themselves with hoses, buckets and hand pumps and started a desperate fight to save their homes. With the canals and ponds completely dried up by a drought, they dug 10-foot-deep holes into the earth in search of groundwater.

“The flames were about 10 meters (30 feet) high, and all we could see was red,” Mr. Akoi told me when I visited him last week, pointing to the goose bumps rising on his arms. “The smoke was so thick and wind was so strong. Our lungs hurt, our eyes burned, but we had to keep going.”

Although they eventually received help and saved their homes, what Mr. Akoi, 38, and his neighbors battled in late August was more than a natural disaster — it was also a man-made calamity produced by years of deliberate land clearing for cash crops, including timber and palm oil.

He lives in Kubu Raya regency in West Kalimantan Province, which contains millions of acres of peatlands, a kind of wetland. Across Indonesia, which shares Borneo with Malaysia and Brunei, the conversion of these bogs into farmland has dried them out and transformed them into tinder boxes. So far this year wildfires have incinerated tens of thousands of acres in this province alone, fueled by an unforgiving drought brought by a powerful El Niño climate shift.

In Pontianak, the provincial capital, Tresna Waniati, a 33-year-old volunteer firefighter, was ready for her next deployment despite having just been discharged from the hospital for a severe respiratory infection. For the past three months, she had been inhaling carbon-choked air while battling the wildfires, leaving her 4-year-old son at home with her parents. To reach the remote fire hot spots, she navigated rugged terrain on her motorcycle, which was weighed down by water pumps, cans of gasoline and rolls of hoses.

“The fires and the smoke are extraordinary this time,” Ms. Tresna said. “Scarcity of water makes it harder. Of course, we are all exhausted, but we have to do it.”

Millions of people across West Kalimantan have been living for months beneath this stifling blanket of haze. Air quality has repeatedly hit hazardous levels, forcing the authorities to extend a state of emergency. Hundreds of schools have suspended in-person classes while reduced visibility — to a few hundred meters — has brought regional transport to a crawl. Some residents wear face masks, but many said they were fed up with them.

Forest fires occur annually in Indonesia, but this year’s devastation could be among the worst on record. Government figures show that about half a million acres of land burned through July, but the independent platform Nusantara Atlas said the toll through August was 2.2 million acres.

The normally bustling market alleys in Pontianak appeared emptier than usual this month, their sounds muffled by the heavy air. Elisabet, 31, was arranging her dried fish containers, wiping away a fine dusting of soot that had settled on the display trays. A few hurried shoppers moved briskly, eager to grab staples before retreating indoors to escape the amber haze that blanketed the city and turned afternoon skies into a murky twilight. Since the haze took hold of the city around late June, she said, her daily sales had dropped by nearly half.

“I know breathing in this toxic air is bad for my health, but I cannot afford to stay home,” said Elisabet, who like many Indonesians goes by one name. “I’m just hoping for a few sales so my goods don’t go to waste.”

The Center of Economic and Law Studies, an Indonesian think tank, estimates that the country’s wildfires from January to August could inflict up to 123.1 trillion rupiah, or about $6.9 billion, in economic and health care costs, a figure expected to climb if the burning continues through the end of the year.

The human toll is also severe. More than 13 million people across seven provinces have been exposed to toxic smoke. According to the Health Ministry, the number of people suffering respiratory infections in these regions more than doubled over a week in September, as the number of hot spots soared. Between Aug. 18 and Sept. 21, health officials recorded nearly 175,000 cases. About a quarter of these were children under 5 years old.

The Muhammadiyah Disaster Management Center, a nonprofit, has set up 13 “Oxygen Houses” where the public can get medical care and oxygen therapy for respiratory distress caused by smoke inhalation. In addition, two mobile units provide oxygen to people in fire zones who are unable to leave or could not afford to evacuate.

“Our volunteers deliver oxygen tanks to the vulnerable or too ill people in the impacted zones,” said Hermayani Putera, the center’s coordinator. “The Oxygen Houses serve as a refuge, clean air sanctuary — a break from the polluted smoke.”

With the haze spreading to neighboring Singapore, Malaysia and the Philippines, Indonesia’s president, Prabowo Subianto, has accepted international assistance from Japan and Malaysia to tackle the fires. He has also ordered a major crackdown on commercial “slash-and-burn” agriculture, in which companies clear forests and burn the fallen trees to make way for new fields.

So far, the Forestry Ministry has suspended the permits of 26 companies that have cut forests to grow cash crops. The authorities are investigating multiple companies on possible criminal charges, warning that they could permanently lose their permits and face massive fines, among other punishments.

However, environmental groups argue that these measures offer little relief to hard-hit regions like West Kalimantan, where policy enforcement has been lax despite previous moratoriums on forest clearing and mandates to protect and restore peatland.

“Many of the fires occurred in peat ecosystems where companies with permits operate,” said Indra Syahnanda, head of advocacy and campaigns at WALHI West Kalimantan, a conservation group. “It is the government’s job to ensure these companies comply with the rules and regulations. Having it on paper does not mean they are applied in the field.”

Instead of going after companies pursuing cash crops, conservationists say the Indonesian government often blames Indigenous communities, which have traditionally practiced slash-and-burn farming methods, for igniting blazes. Members of the Indigenous Dayak communities say that their methods of clearing small plots of lands and building firebreaks have served them well for generations. Crucially, they add, they never clear out flammable peatland.

“It hurts to be accused and made into scapegoats when we strictly adhere to our local wisdom,” said Mr. Akoi, who is Dayak.

But the suffering from the fires is universal. Many in the community experiencing chronic coughing fits and shortness of breath.

“We miss breathing in fresh air and seeing clear sky,” Mr. Akoi said. “All we can do is place our hope in God and our ancestors.”
